The two accent edges B–D and C–D are a smallest set of edges whose removal separates B from E. The card shows that cut and its size 2." width="100%"} Computes the minimum number of edges that must be removed to disconnect the source from the sink. Uses the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm with BFS (Edmonds-Karp) to find maximum flow, which equals the minimum cut by the max-flow min-cut theorem. Equivalently, the result is the maximum number of edge-disjoint paths from source to sink. By default every edge has capacity `1`, even on weighted graphs, so the answer is a count of edges; parallel edges count separately. With `capacity=` the answer is instead the total capacity of the cheapest cut, as in `minimum_cut()`. For undirected graphs, edges are treated as bidirectional. For directed graphs, only paths that follow edge direction from `source=` to `target=` count, so swapping the two can change the answer. Use this to measure how many independent links connect two specific nodes, for example how many cable failures two data centers can tolerate before losing contact. If the nodes are already disconnected the result is `0`. To get the edges themselves, use `minimum_edge_cut()`; for the minimum over all pairs, use `edge_connectivity()`. The method does not modify the graph. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node on the source side of the cut, given as an integer node ID or a string label. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node on the sink side of the cut, given as an integer node ID or a string label. Must be a different node than `source=`. [capacity]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of an edge attribute to use as capacity (`"weight"` also accepts the edge weight of a weighted graph); every edge must hold a numeric value for it. If `None` (default), every edge has capacity `1`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [int | float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Size of the minimum cut: the number of edges to remove (`int`), or with `capacity=` their total capacity (`float`). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If source or sink node doesn't exist, if they're the same, or if an edge lacks the attribute named by `capacity=`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} In a simple chain `A - B - C - D` every edge is a bottleneck, so the minimum cut between the two ends is just 1: ::: {#245576a3 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D")]) ) graph.minimum_cut_value("A", "D") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: Closing the chain into a cycle adds a second, independent route from `A` to `D`, so two edges must now be cut: ::: {#a290a7c9 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.add_edge("D", "A") graph.minimum_cut_value("A", "D") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 2 ``` ::: ::: On a directed graph the cut depends on direction. In the chain `A -> B -> C`, one edge separates `A` from `C`, while `C` cannot reach `A` at all, giving a cut of `0`: ::: {#9055e0c4 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C")]) ) graph.minimum_cut_value("A", "C"), graph.minimum_cut_value("C", "A") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (1, 0) ``` ::: :::
